summary: This informational RFC defines version 2 of the xml2rfc vocabulary, the XML-based language used to write RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It records the vocabulary as implemented by tools and used by the RFC Editor around 2014 and obsoletes RFC 2629. It was replaced by RFC 7991.

eli5.summary: RFC authors write in a special markup language so a program can turn it into a finished document. This describes the rules of that language as it stood around 2014.

questions: how to write an rfc in xml
subtitle: The XML vocabulary that RFC authors use to write Internet-Drafts and RFCs.

tldr.problem: RFC authors need a way to write documents that can be automatically converted into plain text, HTML, and other formats. Having a standardized markup language simplifies authoring and ensures consistent output.
tldr.mechanism: The xml2rfc vocabulary is an XML-based language that describes the structure of an RFC: its front matter (title, authors, abstract), main sections, lists, code samples, references, and metadata. Tools can parse this XML and generate the final document in multiple formats.
tldr.outcome: The v2 vocabulary standardized the state of xml2rfc as of 2014. It was replaced by RFC 7991 (v3) with a simplified vocabulary suitable for modern publication workflows.

today: RFC 7749 is an Informational RFC from February 2016 that was obsoleted by RFC 7991 in December 2016. It defined the xml2rfc v2 vocabulary; RFC 7991 provides the v3 vocabulary with a simplified markup suitable for modern RFC publication workflows. Tools and repositories using xml2rfc still implement v2 for backward compatibility.

sections.title: What Is xml2rfc?
sections.content:
xml2rfc is an XML-based language for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts. RFC authors write their documents in XML according to the xml2rfc vocabulary, and then tools (called processors) transform that XML into finished documents in plain text, HTML, PDF, and other formats.

Version 2 of the vocabulary, defined in this RFC, represents the state of xml2rfc as it was implemented by multiple tools and used by the RFC Editor around 2014. It obsoletes the original version (RFC 2629) with extensions and improvements made over the years. The vocabulary includes 44 different elements, each with specific attributes and allowed content.
sections.eli5: RFC authors mark up their text with special tags to say what is a title, what is a paragraph, what is code, and so on. A program reads these tags and makes a pretty document.

sections.title: How an RFC Document Is Organized
sections.content:
An xml2rfc document follows a standard three-part structure. The <front> element contains the front matter: the title, author information (names, affiliations, addresses), abstract, and metadata such as the RFC category, submission type, and intended area. The <middle> element contains the main body of the document, organized as numbered sections that can be nested to any depth. The <back> element contains back matter: references, appendices, and acknowledgments.

The root element is <rfc>, which wraps the entire document. This element carries attributes that control how the document is rendered, such as the RFC number, submission type (IETF, IAB, IRTF), intended status (Standards Track, Informational, Experimental, Historic), and intellectual property rights declarations.
sections.eli5: A document has three main parts: the front (title and author info), the middle (the actual text in sections), and the back (references and extra stuff). All of this goes inside one main tag.

sections.title: Elements for Writing Content
sections.content:
The vocabulary provides elements for the most common content types. The <t> element represents a paragraph of text. Paragraphs can contain inline formatting with <strong>, <em>, <code>, and <spanx> elements for emphasis, italics, literal text, and styled text.

Structured content uses <list> elements, which can be ordered (numbered), unordered (bulleted), or descriptive (term and definition pairs). <figure> elements wrap diagrams, code samples, and examples. The <artwork> element is special: it preserves all whitespace and line breaks, making it suitable for code, ABNF notation, message diagrams, and ASCII art. <texttable> elements provide simple tables with rows and columns.
sections.eli5: Paragraphs, lists, figures, and tables use different tags. Code and diagrams use a special tag that keeps spaces and line breaks exactly as written.

sections.title: References, Citations, and Cross-References
sections.content:
The <references> element in the back matter contains bibliographic entries. Each <reference> element describes one source, with <front> (title and author), <seriesInfo> (RFC number, series, or other identification), and optional <annotation> (additional commentary).

Throughout the document, <xref> elements create cross-references to sections within the same document or to figures and tables. <eref> elements link to external URLs. <iref> elements create entries for the document's index. <cref> elements are comments and notes meant for editor review during authoring; they do not appear in the final published document.
sections.eli5: References list the sources mentioned in the document. Cross-references point to other parts of the same document or to external links. Special tags let authors add notes for reviewers.

sections.title: Attributes and Document Metadata
sections.content:
Most elements support attributes that control their behavior. The <rfc> root element has attributes like number (the assigned RFC number), category (Standards Track, Informational, Experimental, Historic), ipr (intellectual property rights declarations such as trust200902), and consensus (whether the document represents consensus). The <date> element in the front matter specifies month and year of publication.

List elements use style attributes to specify ordered, unordered, or descriptive presentation. Figure and artwork elements use attributes to control alignment, height, width, and type (for syntax highlighting). The <spanx> element uses a style attribute to apply font styles. Text elements can use hangText to create hanging indentation in lists.
sections.eli5: Tags have attributes that control how they look and behave. You can say a list is numbered or bulleted, whether artwork should be centered, and lots of other details.

sections.title: Version 2 and Beyond
sections.content:
Version 2 of xml2rfc evolved from the original version (v1, RFC 2629) with many extensions and refinements made between 1998 and 2014. The RFC documents major changes: several v1 elements were removed, defaults were changed for some attributes, and new elements were added for better document structure support. Appendix B of the RFC details these changes for authors familiar with v1.

The RFC includes a complete formal schema for validation in RELAX NG Compact Notation (Appendix C), allowing tools to automatically check whether an xml2rfc document is valid. The vocabulary was later superseded by RFC 7991 (v3), which simplified the markup further and aligned it with modern RFC publication practices. This RFC remains the reference for the v2 vocabulary as used by tools and repositories that have not yet migrated to v3.
sections.eli5: Version 2 started from an older version and added features. Version 3 came later with more improvements. This document describes version 2 so people know the rules if they are using it.
